class.name: FE101: Introduction to modern JavaScript & TypeScript

lessons.title: Why JavaScript?
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
JavaScript is the language of the web. Every browser can already run it, so it powers everything you click and see on websites. With Node.js it also runs on servers.

KEY IDEAS
1. Every major browser has a JavaScript engine built in; nothing to install.
2. Client side (browser): what users see and touch: buttons, forms, animations, live updates, chat.
3. Server side (Node.js): logins, storing data, talking to databases, tracking scores.
4. Modern JavaScript: the language as it evolved after the 2015 "ES6" update; what real projects use today.

KEY POINTS
- Python leads in AI and data science; JavaScript leads in web interfaces and can also run servers.
- Example: a game site's interface when you log in is client-side JavaScript; saving your scores is server-side work.

NOTE
Lesson 1, "Welcome to FE101", had no notes. Class dates: Feb 23 – Mar 2.

lessons.title: Hello JavaScript
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
print("Hello") in Python is console.log("Hello"); in JavaScript. Each statement ends with a semicolon.

CODE
```text
Python                 | JavaScript
-----------------------|------------------------------
print("Hello")         | console.log("Hello");
a new line ends a line | a semicolon ; ends a statement
```

```javascript
console.log("Hello");
console.log("World");
```

KEY POINTS
- console.log shows the message in the console, without the quotes.
- One console.log per line of output.
- An embedded editor first means no installs and instant feedback; real browser tools come later.

lessons.title: Variables: const and let
Basic Types & Strings: JavaScript vs Python
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
JavaScript has strings, numbers and booleans, like Python, but only one number type for whole and decimal values. If either side of + is a string, JavaScript glues text together instead of doing math.

CODE
```text
Type     | Examples            | typeof gives | Python
---------|---------------------|--------------|--------------------
String   | "hello", "42"       | "string"     | str
Number   | 5, 3.14, 1000       | "number"     | int and float both
Boolean  | true, false         | "boolean"    | bool
```

```javascript
console.log(5 + 1);              // 6
console.log("5" + 1);            // "51"
console.log("5" + 100);          // "5100"
console.log(typeof (5 + 1));     // "number"
console.log(typeof ("5" + 1));   // "string"
console.log(typeof true);        // "boolean"
```

KEY POINTS
- If either side of + is a string, the number becomes text and the two are joined (concatenation).
- typeof checks a value's type while the code runs: handy for catching "5" where you expected 5.

lessons.title: Conditionals: Python vs JavaScript
Template Literals
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Backtick strings (template literals) let you drop values into text with ${...}, like Python's f-strings. They can also span several lines.

CODE
```javascript
const name = "Tunacan";
console.log(`Hello ${name}`);          // Hello Tunacan
const a = 4, b = 6;
console.log(`Total: ${a + b}`);        // Total: 10

const story = `You enter the spire
your surroundings become pitch black
the floor shakes, you fall into the dark!`;
console.log(story);

console.log('Hello ${name}');          // single quotes: prints Hello ${name} literally
```

KEY POINTS
- Python f"Hello {name}" ↔ JavaScript `Hello ${name}`.
- Anything inside ${ } runs as JavaScript: a variable, a property, an expression.
- Single, double and backtick strings are all type "string"; only backticks interpolate.
- Normal quotes can't hold a bare line break (SyntaxError); backticks can.

lessons.title: Challenge: JS Basics
Equality and Missing Values
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Compare with ===, which checks value and type. == converts types first and causes surprising matches. undefined means "nothing was set"; null means "empty on purpose". Six values count as false in an if.

CODE
```javascript
console.log("5" === 5);           // false (string vs number)
console.log("5" == 5);            // true  ("5" converted to 5)
console.log(0 == false);          // true
console.log(undefined == null);   // true  (special case)
console.log(undefined === null);  // false

let a;
console.log(a);                   // undefined: never given a value
let movementState = null;         // exists, but inactive for now (like Python's None)
```

```javascript
if ("0") console.log("runs");     // non-empty string → truthy
if ("") console.log("never");     // empty string → falsy
```

KEY POINTS
- Use === almost always.
- Falsy: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN (also -0 and 0n). Everything else is truthy, including "0", "false" and -1.
- When an if doesn't run, check whether the value is one of the falsy six.

lessons.title: Arrays (JS Lists)
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
JavaScript arrays are Python lists: square brackets, indexes from 0, .length instead of len(), .push() instead of append(), and .pop() works the same.

CODE
```text
Python              | JavaScript
--------------------|---------------------------
my_list = [1, 2]    | const myList = [1, 2];
len(my_list)        | myList.length
my_list.append(x)   | myList.push(x)
my_list.pop()       | myList.pop()
my_list[-1]         | myList.at(-1)   or   myList[myList.length - 1]
```

```javascript
const playList = ["In Your Eye", "Down Low"];
playList.push("Elevator Up");             // returns the new length, 3
const removed = playList.pop();           // "Elevator Up"
console.log(playList);                    // [ 'In Your Eye', 'Down Low' ]
console.log(playList.length);             // 2
```

KEY POINTS
- const means the name can't be reassigned; the array's contents can still change.
- myList[-1] is undefined in JavaScript; use .at(-1).
- push + pop = a stack (last in, first out).

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A JavaScript object stores named values (properties), like a Python dictionary. You read and change properties with dot notation (enemy.hp) or bracket notation (enemy["hp"]). Brackets let the key come from a variable.

KEY IDEAS
1. Object literal: curly braces, key: value pairs, commas between pairs.
2. Keys usually don't need quotes when they're simple names.
3. Dot notation reads or updates a property whose name you know: enemy.hp.
4. Bracket notation uses a string: enemy["hp"], or a variable holding the string: enemy[key].
5. A missing property returns undefined. There's no error (like Python's dict.get() returning None).
6. Keys are case-sensitive: enemy.Name and enemy.name are different properties.
7. A plain object is just a data container. Classes, methods and "this" (object-oriented programming) come later.

STEPS
To update a property and see the new value:
1. Assign with = (not ==).
2. Then log it. Logging before the update shows the old value.

CODE
```javascript
let enemy = { name: "Viper", hp: 50, status: "poisoned" };

console.log(enemy.name);     // Viper
enemy.hp = 40;               // update with dot notation
console.log(enemy.hp);       // 40

let key = "status";
enemy[key] = "stunned";      // update with bracket notation + a variable
console.log(enemy[key]);     // stunned

console.log(enemy.mana);     // undefined (property doesn't exist)
console.log(enemy.Name);     // undefined (keys are case-sensitive)
```

```python
# Python comparison
data = {"name": "Viper"}
print(data.get("status"))    # None
# data["status"] would raise a KeyError
```

KEY POINTS
- enemy[key] uses the variable's value; enemy["key"] looks for a property literally named "key".
- enemy[status] without quotes looks for a variable named status, which may not exist.
- = assigns a value; == only compares, so player["hp"] == 90 changes nothing.
- Pick one naming style for keys (usually lowercase, like hp and name) and stick with it.
- Missing property → undefined, but reading a property OF undefined crashes: enemy.stats.hp throws a TypeError when stats doesn't exist.

NOTE
console.log(Magic) failed with "Magic is not defined" because, without enemy., JavaScript looks for a variable called Magic. Use enemy.Magic.
